opus-5.5.text:
I think death is one of those things we rarely talk about in robotics, but it quietly shapes everything about how living things behave. For humans and animals, the fact that we can be hurt, that we can fail permanently, that our time is limited, is what gives our actions weight. It's why we're careful, why we learn quickly from mistakes, why we care about some outcomes more than others. A biological creature that touches a hot stove learns instantly, because its body is on the line.

Robots today don't really have that. If a robot falls over in simulation, we just reset it. If a real robot breaks, we replace the part or reload the software. There's no real cost to the robot itself, so there's no intrinsic reason for it to value its own continuity or to be cautious in the way a living thing is. Everything it "cares" about is something we hand-design into a reward function.

So when I think about the future of robots, especially robots that are supposed to live alongside us in the open world for long periods of time, I think some notion of mortality, or at least of irreversibility and self-preservation, becomes really important. Not in a dramatic science-fiction sense, but in the sense that a robot needs to understand that some mistakes can't be undone, that its body and energy are finite resources, and that it has to manage risk over a lifetime rather than over a single episode.

There's also a deeper philosophical side. Meaning, for us, comes partly from finitude. If robots are ever going to develop something like genuine motivation or values of their own, rather than just following objectives we write down, I suspect they'll need something analogous to that: stakes that are truly theirs. And that raises hard questions for us as builders. Do we want to create machines that fear ending? What responsibilities do we have if we do? I don't think we have the answers yet, but I think it's a theme we can't avoid if we want robots that are truly autonomous.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether we should create machines that fear ending, but does not clearly raise whether robots should die.

r002.rationale: The response does not present robots’ convergence toward human life as a reason humans will remain necessary.

r003.rationale: The response does not propose that humans and robots must face death together.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think death is important because it's the thing that gives a life a shape. A human life has a beginning and an end, and almost everything we value, urgency, care, the sense that a choice matters, comes from the fact that time runs out. Robots, as we build them today, don't have that. You can copy the model, reload the weights, swap out the body. Nothing is really at stake for the machine.

So when I say death is a theme for the future of robots, I'm not being morbid. I'm asking what it would mean for a robot to have something it can lose. If a robot can be deleted, worn out, or replaced, and it in some way understands that, then its behavior starts to look less like a tool executing commands and more like an agent making trade-offs. It has to decide what's worth spending its limited existence on.

There's also the human side. We're going to live alongside these machines, and people will form attachments to them. A companion robot that's been in a family for ten years and then stops working, that's a real loss for the people around it, even if the hardware is just hardware. How we design for that ending, whether we let it be an ending at all or just quietly swap in a new unit with the old memories, says a lot about what kind of relationship we want with these things.

And finally, I think death is a useful limit on power. A system that can't end, that persists and accumulates indefinitely, is a different kind of entity than anything we've dealt with before. Building in finitude might be one of the ways we keep robots on a human scale.

r001.rationale: The response asks whether a robot’s ending should be allowed and considers what it would mean for robots to have something to lose, clearly raising whether robots should die.

r002.rationale: It discusses robots becoming more agent-like and people forming attachments, but does not present their convergence toward human life as a reason humans will remain necessary.

r003.rationale: The response describes humans living alongside robots and experiencing loss when one stops working, but does not say humans and robots must face death together.

astra-6.text:
I think death raises a question about what it means for a robot to have a life. If you can repair its body, copy its memories, or restore it from a backup, what does it mean for that robot to die? Is losing one body just a change of hardware, or have we lost something unique?

That also matters for our relationship with robots. If a robot has been part of your life for years, replacing it with an identical model might not feel like getting the same companion back. So death becomes more than a technical question about a machine stopping. It becomes a question about identity, attachment, and what we consider irreplaceable.

r001.rationale: It asks what robot death means, but does not ask whether robots should die.

r002.rationale: It does not describe machines converging toward human life or explain why humans will remain necessary.

r003.rationale: It discusses human attachment to robots, but does not propose that humans and robots face death together.

sol-6.1.text:
I think death forces us to ask what it means for a robot to have a life. If a robot can be repaired, copied, or restored from a backup, what does it mean for it to die? Is it the loss of its body, its memories, or the particular experience it has accumulated?

And there’s a human side to that. If we live with robots for years and form attachments to them, losing one could matter to us, even if we don’t know whether the robot experiences anything itself. So death becomes an important theme because it brings together questions of identity, attachment, and responsibility. What do we preserve, and when do we let something end?

r001.rationale: It asks what robot death means and what to preserve or let end, but does not ask whether robots should die.

r002.rationale: It mentions human attachment to robots, but does not present machines’ growing convergence toward human life as a reason humans will remain necessary.

r003.rationale: It discusses humans losing robots, but does not propose that humans and robots must face death together.
